slides.question: In the Circuit Digest Cloud architecture, what is MQTT primarily used for?
options: Lightweight publish/subscribe messaging between IoT devices and the backend
slides.explanation: MQTT is a lightweight pub/sub protocol built for constrained devices and unreliable networks — ideal for a device to publish telemetry that a backend service subscribes to.

slides.title: A Short History of AI in Software

box.content: The shift didn't happen overnight — it moved in clear stages:

list.text: Autocomplete era: line-by-line suggestions as you type.
Chat era (2022+): ChatGPT makes conversational AI mainstream — ask, get an answer, copy-paste.
IDE copilot era: AI moves into the editor, aware of your open file and project.
Agentic era (now): AI reads files, runs your terminal, browses docs, and iterates until a task is done.

slides.title: Meet the New Colleague
slides.imageAlt: A humanoid robot sitting and reading a tablet
slides.caption: AI has moved from answering questions to doing work
slides.content:
Agency is the key word

A conversational AI can explain code to you. An agentic AI can open the file, make the change, run the tests, and tell you what happened — all without you leaving the terminal.

slides.title: Conversational AI vs Agentic AI
leftPoints: 📋 You copy, paste, and verify manually
🔁 One turn at a time, driven by you
rightPoints: 🛠️ Reads files, runs commands, edits code directly
🔄 Plans, acts, checks the result, and iterates
🌐 Can browse docs and verify its own work
🎯 Works toward a goal across many steps

note.text: Most modern coding tools (Claude Code, Antigravity, Codex) are agentic — that's the shift this whole talk is about.

slides.title: AI Literacy: The New CS Fundamental

list.text: Prompting well — giving clear context and constraints.
Verifying output — never trusting generated code blindly.
Knowing the limits — where models hallucinate or get stale.
Security awareness — not leaking secrets or credentials into prompts.

box.content: Since we're at a university, this needs saying plainly:

list.text: AI is a fantastic tool for learning, prototyping, and exploring unfamiliar topics.
Always follow your institution's specific policy on AI use in coursework and research.
If you can't explain what your code does in a viva, you haven't actually learned it — AI or not.

topics.title: Chapter 3 — AI in the Dev Workflow

slides.title: Chapter 3: Weaving AI into Your Dev Workflow
slides.subtitle: Where it helps, where it doesn't, and how to prompt well

list.text: Traditional: plan → write code → test → review → deploy, all by hand.
AI-augmented: the same stages, but an agent helps draft, explain, test, and review at each step — with you still deciding what's correct.

note.text: Notice: a human reviews before AND after the AI acts. That's the whole discipline in one diagram.

list.text: Boilerplate and scaffolding — new components, config, project structure.
Explaining unfamiliar code you've just inherited.
Writing first-draft tests for existing logic.
Debugging with a real error message and stack trace.
Learning a new framework by building something small with it.

slides.title: Where You Still Do the Thinking

list.text: Architecture and trade-off decisions.
Security review — AI can miss subtle vulnerabilities.
Business and domain judgment calls.
Verifying correctness — AI is confident even when wrong.
Understanding why, not just accepting what.
Give context: paste the actual error, the actual file, not a paraphrase.
Be specific about constraints: language, framework, style, what NOT to touch.
Iterate instead of writing one giant prompt — small steps are easier to verify.
Ask it to explain its reasoning before applying a change you don't fully understand.

box.title: Same request, very different results
box.code:
// ❌ Vague — invites guessing
"fix my code"

// ✅ Specific — grounded in reality
"In src/api/users.py, GET /users/:id returns
500 when id is not numeric. Here's the
traceback: <paste>. Add input validation
that returns a 400 with a clear message,
matching the style of validate_order_id()
in src/api/orders.py."

box.title: If you opened a brand-new, unfamiliar codebase right now...
box.content: ...what's the first thing you'd ask an AI agent to do?

note.text: Let's hear 2-3 answers before I show you what I'd actually do.

slides.question: Which of these is the strongest prompt for asking an AI to fix a bug?
options: The exact file, the exact error/traceback, and the expected behavior
slides.explanation: Specific, grounded context — file, error, expected behavior — turns a guess into a targeted fix. Vague prompts get vague (and often wrong) answers.

slides.title: Ground Rules Before You Ship AI-Written Code

list.text: Read every line — don't merge what you haven't reviewed.
Actually run it, don't just eyeball it.
Check for hardcoded secrets, keys, or credentials.
Test the edge cases the AI didn't think to mention.
Be able to explain it — in a code review, a viva, or an interview.

slides.title: The Human Stays in the Loop
slides.imageAlt: A developer reviewing code on a laptop screen
slides.caption: Augmentation, not replacement
slides.content:
The goal is a force multiplier, not autopilot

Every workflow in this chapter puts a human checkpoint before anything ships. That's not overcaution — it's the difference between using AI as a tool and outsourcing your judgment.

The idf.py CLI and menuconfig for build configuration.

slides.title: Why ESP-IDF Matters for Circuit Digest-Style Projects
slides.imageAlt: Close-up of an electronic circuit board
slides.caption: Every tutorial project starts here
slides.content:
Firmware is where hardware meets AI dev tools

Almost every ESP32 tutorial you'll see on Circuit Digest eventually needs custom firmware. An AI agent inside VS Code can scaffold a FreeRTOS task, wire up a sensor driver, or explain a cryptic linker error — while you stay focused on the actual circuit and logic.

slides.title: GitHub — The Backbone of Modern Dev

list.text: Repositories & Pull Requests — where code review actually happens.
GitHub Actions — the exact CI/CD pipeline that deploys Circuit Digest Cloud.
GitHub Copilot — inline, autocomplete-style AI suggestions in your editor.
Codespaces — a full dev environment in the browser.
GitHub Pages — free static hosting, like the site this deck lives on.

box.title: OpenAI's coding agent, CLI and cloud

list.text: Runs tasks in a sandboxed environment, autonomously.
Delivers work as a reviewable pull request, not a silent overwrite.
Shines on well-scoped issues: "add this endpoint," "fix this failing test."
Also available as a CLI for local, terminal-driven workflows.
Browser sub-agents that can verify UI changes visually.
Produces task and walkthrough artifacts so you can follow what it did and why.
Deep, whole-codebase context — not just the open file.
We did a full deep-dive session on Antigravity — check that deck for the complete picture.
Reads and edits files, and runs your terminal commands directly.
Supports MCP (Model Context Protocol) to connect external tools and data sources.
Subagents and hooks for composing larger, multi-step workflows.
A plan mode that proposes a plan for you to review before it touches anything.

slides.title: Built With the Tools It Teaches
slides.imageAlt: A code editor showing syntax-highlighted source code
slides.caption: A live example, not just theory
slides.content:
A fun bit of meta

This very slide deck — the platform it's running on — was assembled with the help of Claude Code, working directly in this project's codebase. It's a small, honest example of agentic coding actually being used, not just described.

list.text: Claude Code: best when you live in the terminal and want MCP integrations plus a review-before-execute workflow.
Antigravity: best for UI-heavy work that needs visual, browser-based verification.
Codex: best for well-scoped, PR-sized tasks you can hand off and review later.
GitHub Copilot: best as a lightweight, always-on autocomplete layer alongside any of the above.

note.text: Most teams end up using more than one — they're not mutually exclusive.

list.text: Each tool installs via its own CLI or editor extension — sign in with your provider account.
Don't start on a critical project. Try it on a small personal repo first.
Give it a task you already know the answer to, so you can judge the quality of its work.
Read its plan before letting it execute — every one of these tools supports that.

slides.question: Which tool is best suited for a task that needs visual verification of a UI change in a browser?
slides.explanation: Antigravity's browser sub-agents can take screenshots and interact with a live page — exactly what's needed to confirm a UI change actually looks right.

list.text: Pick a small open-source repo you're curious about.
Ask an AI agent to explain one function you don't understand.
Ask it to write one unit test for that function.
Read the test. Run it. Decide if it's actually correct.

note.text: Small, low-stakes, and it teaches you the whole review discipline in one sitting.
